title: Apollonia (9 February)
hookLine: an older woman martyred in Alexandria, remembered in a bishop's letter; patron of dentists

lines: A WOMAN HOLDING PLIERS AND A TOOTH.
cards: A bishop in Alexandria writes to a fellow bishop about what he has just lived through: riots in his city, Christians dragged from their homes, beaten, killed in the streets.
In the middle of his list he stops on one name, an older woman, and tells what the mob did to her. Later, painters would show her standing calmly with a pair of pliers, and in the pliers, a tooth.
It looks almost comic until you know why. That letter is how we know Apollonia.

teach.b: The bishop was Dionysius of Alexandria, and the historian Eusebius copied part of his letter into his Church History. Here's what Dionysius says, in plain words. A mob turned on the city's Christians.
They seized Apollonia, whom he calls a marvelous older woman, a virgin. They beat her and broke out her teeth.

teach.h: A MOB, A FIRE, A CHOICE.
teach.b: Then they built a fire outside the city and told her to say their blasphemies or be burned alive. She asked for a moment. They let her go.
And she stepped into the fire herself. That's the whole account, a few lines in a letter.
Later writers asked hard questions about that last step, and the Church has still honored her as a martyr who would not deny Christ.

The teeth explain the pliers, and the pliers explain the dentists: in time, people with toothache asked her prayers, and dentists took her as a patron. A strange road from a riot to a dental office, but a real one.
A mob cornered an older woman, and she did not give way.

teach.h: CAST ME NOT OFF IN THE TIME OF OLD AGE.
teach.b: Psalm seventy has an old person's prayer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Cast me not off in the time of old age: when my strength shall fail, do not thou forsake me." Look back at this week: Vincent speaking for his bishop.
Francis de Sales sliding pages under doors. Timothy and Titus, trusted young. Angela teaching the girls.
Blaise and the candles. Agatha of Sicily. And Apollonia, old, cornered, and faithful.

how: Catholics remember Saint Apollonia in February; she appears in art holding pliers with a tooth, and dentists and people with toothache ask her prayers.

o: a Greek goddess of healing and medicine
an older martyr of Alexandria, patron of dentists
a young nun who founded a hospital in Egypt

p: the bishop who wrote the letter
copied it into his Church History

s: Apollonia was a young girl when she died
Dionysius calls her an older woman, a virgin.
we know her story from a letter by a bishop of her own city
Dionysius of Alexandria, quoted by Eusebius.
dentists took her as patron because the mob broke out her teeth.

games.q: you're Apollonia. the mob has built a fire and tells you to say their blasphemies or burn. what do you do?
o: ask for a moment, then step into the fire yourself.
stay silent and let them decide.
games.why: Dionysius says she asked for a moment, was let go, and stepped into the fire herself.

practice: Run your tongue along your teeth: they chew, help you speak, let you smile. Bring to mind whoever has cared for them, a dentist, a hygienist, a parent who made you brush, and then an older person you know, and their strength.
If you pray, ask Saint Apollonia to pray for them and for anyone in pain tonight; if you don't, hold them with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Apollonia. An older woman of Alexandria who would not deny Christ before a mob. Her story is in a bishop's letter, and dentists honor her as a patron.

carryVoice: Your line: she kept faith. A few lines in a letter kept her name alive. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

sources.q: Cast me not off in the time of old age: when my strength shall fail, do not thou forsake me.

sources.ref: Eusebius, Church History 6.41 (letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Fabius)
